The Eastern common cuscus Phalanger intercastellanus is a medium-sized arboreal marsupial inhabiting the lowland rainforests of eastern Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands. Studies on captive individuals have provided detailed insight into the species' basic physiological parameters. At a body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the resting metabolic rate of adults reaches approximately 658.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 658.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns with predictions for a folivore-frugivore of its body mass. This metabolic measurement, derived from flow-through respirometry trials, underscores the relatively low energetic demands typical of arboreal marsupials subsisting on a diet that includes leaves, fruits, and occasional flowers. The species is relatively long-lived for a possum of its size; the maximum lifespan recorded in captivity, based on the congeneric spotted cuscus Spilocuscus maculatus, is approximately 6,899 days [am = approximately 6,899 days] under the same thermoneutral conditions, suggesting a slow life-history pace consistent with low reproductive output and extended paren at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]tal investment.

Reproductive parameters for Phalanger intercastellanus have been inferred from closely related congeners due to a paucity of direct field data. Females are thought to produce litters of two pups [N_R_i = litters of two pups], and available evidence from Phalanger orientalis indicates they typically give birth to a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. This low annual fecundity is characteristic of many phalangerid marsupials and likely reflects the energetic constraints of lactation in a seasonally variable rainforest environment. The gestation period, based on observations in Phalanger orientalis, lasts approximately 13 days [tg = approximately 13 days] at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a remarkably short duration for a mammal of this size. After this brief internal development, the altricial neonates make their way to the pouch, where they will complete the bulk of their early growth. The brevity of gestation highlights the marsupials' reliance on extended lactation rather than prolonged intrauterine development.

Neonatal offspring are exceptionally altricial at birth, with a wet weight of just 0.9 grams [Wwb = 0.9 grams], a value comparable to that reported for the congeneric spotted cuscus Spilocuscus maculatus. This minuscule birth mass is typical of marsupials, which deliver highly altricial young after a very short gestation. The nursing period is extensive, with the suckling juvenile remaining continuously attached to a teat within the pouch for many months. Weaning in this species is estimated to occur at 270 days after birth [tx = 270 days after birth], a duration that reflects the prolonged period of milk dependency at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. As females approach their adult size, growth trajectories plateau upon reaching an ultimate body mass of 2,200 grams [Wwi = 2,200 grams], though field records indicate a range from 1.4 to 2.2 kilograms. This maximum adult weight is achieved after a prolonged juvenile and sub-adult phase, during which the young animals continue to refine their foraging skills and spatial knowledge of the home range. Puberty, extrapolated from growth data on Spilocuscus maculatus, is attained at 300 days after birth [tp = 300 days after birth] under stable thermal conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This relatively late onset of sexual maturation is consistent with the species' slow life history, allowing ample time for skeletal growth and the accumulation of sufficient body condition to support the energetic costs of reproduction. The pre-reproductive period is thus a critical window of somatic development.

Comparative analyses with other phalangerid marsupials reveal that the life-history strategy of the Eastern common cuscus is characterized by a pronounced trade-off between offspring size and number.
